extracted.intended_audience: readers/authors/distributors of Project Gutenberg eBooks; readers interested in Descartes' methodological guidance (philosophers, scientists, historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Contains Descartes' methodological principles for discovering and reporting natural-philosophical knowledge (experiments, order of inquiry, publication practices), plus the Project Gutenberg Full License terms governing use, redistribution, format-conversion, fees, and trademark use of the eBook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments increase in necessity as knowledge advances
rubrics_metrics.description: "I remarked, moreover, with respect to experiments, that they become always more necessary the more one is advanced in knowledge; for, at the commencement, it is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses...than to concern ourselves about more uncommon and recondite phenomena".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin inquiry using common, readily observable phenomena and only increasingly rely on designed experiments as one progresses and ordinary causes become understood. Anti-pattern: chasing rare phenomena early, which often mislead while ordinary causes remain unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of inquiry: principles → ordinary effects → particulars (experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have adopted the following order: first, I have essayed to find in general the principles, or first causes of all that is or can be in the world... In the second place, I examined what were the first and most ordinary effects that could be deduced from these causes; and... afterwards... to descend to the more particular... avail ourselves of many particular experiments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical procedure: deduce general principles (from first truths), derive common effects from them, then use experiments to resolve particulars and distinguish among possible modes. This prescribes ascending/descending reasoning combined with experimental checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminating experiments to choose among multiple explanatory modes
rubrics_metrics.description: "my greatest difficulty usually is to discover in which of these modes the effect is dependent upon them; for out of this difficulty cannot otherwise extricate myself than by again seeking certain experiments, which may be such that their result is not the same, if it is in the one of these modes... as it would be if it were to be explained in the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an effect can be deduced in different ways from the principles, design experiments whose outcomes differ depending on which mode is correct. Guidance: choose experiments that yield divergent results under competing explanations; avoid ambiguous tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer phenomena presented to the senses at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: At the commencement it is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses, and of which we cannot remain ignorant... than to concern ourselves about more uncommon and recondite phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early-stage inquiry should focus on obvious, repeatable sensory phenomena to ground principles. Anti-pattern: prioritizing exotic observations before establishing explanations for common cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive causes from effects (ascend to causes through their effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: it is impossible for the human mind to distinguish the forms or species of bodies... unless we rise to causes through their effects, and avail ourselves of many particular experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed effects and controlled experiments to infer plausible causes; this is an iterative inferential strategy rather than speculative taxonomy without experimental grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label hypotheses and explain their role; avoid circularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If some of the matters... I call them hypotheses and seem indifferent about giving proof of them, I request a patient and attentive reading... Nor must it be imagined that I here commit the fallacy... called a circle; for since experience renders the majority of these effects most certain, the causes from which I deduce them do not serve so much to establish their reality as to explain their existence; but on the contrary, the reality of the causes is established by the reality of the effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting conjectural statements, explicitly identify them as hypotheses and show how empirical effects justify or test the purported causes. Avoid circular argument by ensuring effects provide independent confirmation of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate results after testing; avoid premature publication that distracts work
rubrics_metrics.description: I have been led to change my opinion, and to think that I ought indeed to go on committing to writing all the results which I deemed of any moment, as soon as I should have tested their truth... but I resolved by no means to consent to their publication during my lifetime, lest either the oppositions or the controversies to which they might give rise, or even the reputation... should be any occasion of my losing the time that I had set apart for my own improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish findings once tested to the author's satisfaction; balance public benefit against risk of distraction, misuse, or premature dispute. Practical rule: commit tested results to writing; withhold full publication if doing so would impede further necessary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish specimens that avoid unnecessary controversy and excessive disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: I thought that it was easy for me to select some matters which should neither be obnoxious to much controversy, nor should compel me to expound more of my principles than I desired, and which should yet be sufficient clearly to exhibit what I can or cannot accomplish in the sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disclosing work incrementally, choose examples that demonstrate method and results without revealing every foundational principle or provoking unproductive controversy. Use selectivity to present useful, non-misleading specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experiments thoroughly; be wary of poorly described or biased prior experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: the experiments are, for the most part, accompanied with so many circumstances and superfluous elements, as to make it exceedingly difficult to disentangle the truth from its adjuncts--besides, he will find almost all of them so ill described, or even so false (because those who made them have wished to see in them only such facts as they deemed conformable to their principles)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, detailed descriptions of experimental conditions to allow reproducibility and selection. Beware confirmation bias in prior reports and insufficiently documented trials; do not rely uncritically on third-party experiments unless adequately described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer paid, skilled artisans for experimental execution over unpaid volunteers
rubrics_metrics.description: one man is not equal to the task of making them all; but yet he can advantageously avail himself, in this work, of no hands besides his own, unless those of artisans, or parties of the same kind, whom he could pay, and whom the hope of gain (a means of great efficacy) might stimulate to accuracy in the performance of what was prescribed to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use skilled, compensated technicians for precision experimental work when needed. Anti-pattern: relying on unpaid volunteers whose promises may exceed performance and whose motives reduce reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to objections candidly and briefly; publish objections with replies
rubrics_metrics.description: I request all who may have any objections to make to them, to take the trouble of forwarding these to my publisher, who will give me notice of them, that I may endeavor to subjoin at the same time my reply; and in this way readers seeing both at once will more easily determine where the truth lies; for I do not engage in any case to make prolix replies, but only with perfect frankness to avow my errors if I am convinced of them...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite critiques and publish them alongside concise, frank replies to aid readers' judgment. Keep replies focused and avoid prolix defences; if convinced of error, acknowledge it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer discovering truths oneself; cultivate habits of gradual, ordered inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: the habit which they will acquire, by seeking first what is easy, and then passing onward slowly and step by step to the more difficult, will benefit them more than all my instructions... if I had been taught from my youth all the truths... I should never, perhaps, have known any beyond these; at least, I should never have acquired the habit and the facility... in always discovering new truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize learning-by-discovery and incremental difficulty increases rather than rote acceptance of others' formulations. Methodological virtue: stepwise, self-driven inquiry fosters capacity to find new truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the vernacular to reach unprejudiced judges when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: if I write in French, which is the language of my country, in preference to Latin... it is because I expect that those who make use of their unprejudiced natural reason will be better judges of my opinions than those who give heed to the writings of the ancients only...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the language and medium that make work accessible to the intended, fair-minded audience. Rationale: accessibility can improve independent judgment; anti-pattern: using obscure classical languages to gatekeep argument.
